claims.claim: Zero documents queries as the way the developer defines what is read and synced.
claims.title: Queries - Zero docs
claims.quote: Queries are how you read and sync data with Zero.
claims.note: Mechanism name: queries (defined with defineQueries/defineQuery, ZQL expression). Full page text fetched; passages located by search and read in context.

claims.claim: Queries are named; the name is sent to the developer's own server, which returns the ZQL that zero-cache runs.
claims.title: Queries - Zero docs
claims.quote: Zero-cache calls the queries endpoint on your server to get the ZQL for the query.
claims.note: Same page also says: 'Each Query has a queryName which is computed by defineQueries' and 'the server can add extra filters to enforce permissions that the client query does not.' So named queries are resolved by developer-written server code. The page does NOT say whether related rows sync automatically (silent; no relationships text found on this page) - no related-data claim made.

claims.claim: A shape is a table plus an optional where clause (also optional columns), written by the developer.
claims.title: Shapes - Guide
claims.quote: an optional where clause to filter which rows are included in the shape
claims.note: Page lists: 'a table, such as items' + optional where clause + optional columns + optional queryable columns. Old URL electric-sql.com/docs/guides/shapes 301-redirects to electric.ax/docs/guides/shapes (which I read). Mechanism name: Shapes.

claims.claim: Related data across tables is not automatic: the developer defines multiple shapes.
claims.title: Shapes - Guide
claims.quote: For syncing related data across tables, you currently need to use multiple shapes.
claims.note: Same Limitations section: 'the shape only contains rows from the root table - not the related data itself.' Page says the old Electric had include trees; 'The new Electric has not yet implemented support for include trees.'

claims.claim: Sync Streams: the developer writes SQL-like queries defining streams; the client app subscribes to the streams it needs.
claims.title: Sync Streams - PowerSync Documentation
claims.quote: you write SQL-like queries to define streams of data, and your client app subscribes to the streams it needs
claims.note: Mechanism name: Sync Streams (YAML config; each stream has a name and a SQL-like query). Old URL docs.powersync.com/usage/sync-streams redirects here. Page also: 'auto_subscribe: true' makes streams sync on connect.

claims.claim: Related tables are reached by subqueries or joins, but a stream query selects columns from one table; related data is added as further queries in the stream.
claims.title: Writing Queries - PowerSync Documentation
claims.quote: select columns from a single table (e.g. comments.*)
claims.note: Candidate wording 'queries must select related rows' CORRECTED: page says subqueries 'filter based on related tables' and JOIN queries 'select columns from a single table'; example 'project_details' stream lists separate SELECTs for tasks, files, comments under the bullet 'Related data should sync together'. Read via the page's .md rendering.
claims.our_reading: The developer still lists each related table as its own query in the scope.

claims.claim: The sync function is developer-written JavaScript that routes each document to channels with channel().
claims.title: Sync Function API Reference
claims.quote: Use the channel() function to route the document to the named channel(s).
claims.note: Page intro: 'The Sync Function is crucial to the security of data sync and replication. It is in charge of data validation, access control and routing.' Mechanism: sync function + channels. Page also says 'Channels don't have to be predefined.' Page silent on related/linked documents - no related-data claim.

claims.claim: The developer grants users access to channels with access() in the same function.
claims.title: Sync Function API Reference
claims.quote: Use the access() function to grant a user access to a channel.
claims.note: Grants from all documents combine as a union (page text: 'effects of all access calls ... combined in a union').

claims.claim: Ditto devices state what they want to receive with subscription queries written by the developer.
claims.title: Syncing Data - Ditto Documentation
claims.quote: Devices are able to express which data they would like to synchronize using subscription queries.
claims.note: Mechanism: subscription queries (DQL). SDK page https://docs.ditto.live/sdk/latest/sync/syncing-data ('Managing Subscriptions') adds: 'Subscriptions allow you to declaratively describe the data that you want a particular device to receive.'

claims.claim: A subscription query cannot join collections; the developer subscribes to each collection separately.
claims.title: Managing Subscriptions - Ditto Documentation
claims.quote: Subscribe to each collection separately and perform the join in an execute or registerObserver query.
claims.note: Full sentence before it: 'a subscription query that joins collections fails with an unsupported query error.'

claims.claim: In July 2024 ElectricSQL announced a clean rebuild of its sync engine; the previous system was frozen.
claims.title: A new approach to building Electric
claims.quote: Electric Next was a clean rebuild of the Electric sync engine that now forms the basis of ElectricSQL moving forwards.
claims.date_of_source: 2024-07-17 (from the URL path; the post body shows no date line)
claims.note: Same post: 'we froze the old system'. Date taken from the URL /blog/2024/07/17/ and the 1.0 post's statement 'In 2024 we re-built Electric from scratch'. Read via the .md rendering.

claims.claim: Electric 1.0 (GA) was announced in March 2025.
claims.title: Electric 1.0 released
claims.quote: With version 1.0.0, Electric is now in GA. The APIs are stable
claims.note: Quote has the link markup removed: source reads 'With [version 1.0.0](...), Electric is now in GA. The APIs are stable and ...'. Date from URL path.

claims.claim: The post says previously open-sourced Electric projects stay open source.

claims.claim: On 2026-09-22 PowerSync announced it is phasing out Sync Rules in favour of Sync Streams.
claims.title: Our Plan for Phasing Out Sync Rules
claims.quote: We're phasing out Sync Rules over the next 15 months in favor of Sync Streams.
claims.note: Candidate said 'legacy': docs title is 'Sync Rules (Legacy)' and docs/announcement say 'deprecated'. Post: 'Nothing changes for your instance today.' Sync Streams 'in beta since March 2026 and generally available since May 2026'.

claims.claim: Announced timeline: Sync Rules removed from the service in a new major version on 15 September 2027; deploys stop and support ends on 15 December 2027.
claims.title: Our Plan for Phasing Out Sync Rules
claims.quote: Instances still on Sync Rules keep running, but we no longer release security fixes for them. Support for Sync Rules ends.
claims.note: Quote is the 15 December 2027 entry. Also: 'New PowerSync Cloud organizations can only use Sync Streams' from the announcement date. The docs page https://docs.powersync.com/sync/rules/overview says 'Sync Rules are deprecated' and 'Nothing changes for your instance today'.

claims.claim: MongoDB deprecated Atlas Device Sync (with the Device SDKs) in September 2024, with removal on 30 September 2025.
claims.title: Atlas Device SDKs Deprecation
claims.quote: Atlas Device SDKs will reach end-of-life and be removed on September 30, 2025.
claims.date_of_source: 'As of September 2024' (stated in page); no page date line
claims.note: CORRECTION: pages say 'Device Sync' and 'Device SDKs'; the words 'Flexible Sync' and 'Realm Flexible Sync' do not occur on either page I read. Same page: 'The on-device database will continue to exist as an open source project.' and 'apps built using Sync need to move to an alternative solution or remove Sync before September 30, 2025.' Fetched the .md rendering of the page.

claims.claim: The Device Sync deprecation page names alternative providers, including Ditto and PowerSync.

claims.quote: If you use Device Sync, you should migrate to one of the alternative solution providers listed below.

Alternatives listed: Ditto, PowerSync, ObjectBox, AWS AppSync, HiveMQ, Ably, Parse, Cedalo. The community-forum notice (mongodb.com/community/forums/...296687) returned 403, so not used.

Fits 'products change direction' only as a team acquisition; do not say 'retired'.

claims.claim: No official matrix.org source found for a P2P Matrix / Pinecone 'hiatus'.
claims.title: The 2025 Matrix Holiday Special
claims.quote: Element is still hopeful to do some very pragmatic P2P Matrix work in 2026, after an initial spike back in November
claims.note: The word 'hiatus' does not appear in the holiday special. Also, This Week in Matrix 2026-07-10 says 'Matthew announces P2P Matrix is back' - the opposite of a retirement as of today. Dropped as instructed.

claims.claim: A user reported desktop and Android clients not syncing, with the sync status showing 'Incompatible version'.
claims.title: Anytype network "incompatible version" won't update or sync
claims.quote: Anytype network - Incompatible version
claims.read_depth: full page (forum JSON of whole thread, 5 posts)
claims.our_reading: Film may say: a user reported that a protocol update left an older client unable to sync until it was manually updated.
claims.note: User bug report (poster 'deiadora'), not an Anytype statement. A reply the same day (user 'Razor'; role not stated on the thread - do not call staff) says: 'We have updated the protocol, latest version is 0.54.11'; a later reply says download from GitHub/website; poster confirms fixed 2026-04-17 after updating. Poster says in-app Update button did not respond.

claims.claim: A user on desktop 0.53.1 reported new items stuck with spinning sync wheels; intermediate version 0.54.2 still failed and 0.54.11 worked.
claims.title: Anytype Desktop - minimal version supported by Anytype cloud
claims.quote: Update: version 0.54.2 - sync to cloud still not working. version 0.54.11 - sync is finally working.
claims.read_depth: full page (forum JSON of whole thread, 2 posts)
claims.note: User report (poster 'GTX'). Poster's edit note: the sync status showed 'Incompatible version'; asks where to find the oldest supported version - unanswered in thread as fetched (2 posts only). Original title edited by poster from a Bugs post to Help.

claims.claim: Ink & Switch say that with no central database server there is no authoritative current schema, and ask how versions can interoperate as formats evolve.
claims.title: Local-first software: You own your data, in spite of the cloud
claims.quote: As there is no central database server, there is no authoritative “current” schema for the data.
claims.note: Authors Kleppmann, Wiggins, van Hardenberg, McGranaghan; also in Onward! 2019. Adjacent sentences: 'Different collaborators may be using different versions of an application, potentially with different features.' and 'How can we write software so that varying application versions can safely interoperate, even as data formats evolve?' WORDING CORRECTION: the essay frames this as 'interesting problems'/an open question (it says 'we see further interesting problems around types, schema migrations, and compatibility'); it does NOT use the words 'unsolved' or 'difficult' for schema evolution. Say 'an open question they pose', not 'unsolved'.

claims.claim: The essay lists growth of CRDT change history as a performance problem.
claims.title: Local-first software: You own your data, in spite of the cloud
claims.quote: CRDTs accumulate a large change history, which creates performance problems.
claims.note: Same section: history 'can’t easily be truncated because it’s impossible to know when someone might reconnect to your shared document after six months away'; 'We continue to optimize Automerge, but this is a major area of ongoing work.' (Automerge is the authors' own project.)

claims.claim: The essay says peer-to-peer technologies they used were not production-ready, naming NAT traversal as unreliable.
claims.title: Local-first software: You own your data, in spite of the cloud
claims.quote: NAT traversal, in particular, is unreliable depending on the particular router or network topology
claims.note: Context sentence: 'these technologies are nowhere near production-ready'. Separately: 'Network communication remains an unsolved problem.' (this is the one place the essay uses 'unsolved'). 2019 statement about their prototypes - not a 2026 status.

claims.claim: The essay says access control beyond secret links is an open research question.
claims.title: Local-first software: You own your data, in spite of the cloud
claims.quote: Access permissions for documents beyond secret URLs remain an open research question.
claims.note: Also asks: 'If we can’t remove documents from others’ computers, what does it mean to “stop sharing” with someone?' (that exact wording from fetch summary; not separately grep-verified).

claims.claim: The study covers 17.8 million posts, about 1.56 million posting pubkeys and 712 relays with event data, from 1 July to 31 December 2023.
claims.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
claims.quote: We assemble a dataset of 17.8 million posts, 1.5 million unique pubkeys (users), and 712 relays, spanning the time period from 2023-07-01 to 2023-12-31.
claims.read_depth: full page (full PDF text extracted and grepped)
claims.note: CANDIDATE CORRECTIONS: paper text says 17.8M (exact 17,851,871 - rounds to 17.9M, truncated to 17.8M in text) and '1.5 million' (exact 1,558,891 = 1.56M). Use the paper's own '17.8 million' or exact counts. 712 is relays from which event data was retrieved, out of 911 seen online at least once (199 yielded none). v1 (Feb 2024) had a different title/abstract: 'Exploring the Nostr Ecosystem: A Study of Decentralization and Resilience'.

claims.claim: On average each post is stored on 34.6 relays.
claims.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
claims.quote: on average, a post is replicated across 34.6 relays
claims.read_depth: full page (full PDF text extracted and grepped)
claims.note: Also: 616M post replications for 17.8M posts; average 12.4 autonomous systems. Paper frames replication as intended censorship resistance ('decentralized backup') as well as overhead - present both.

claims.claim: The study estimates 98.2% of download traffic is redundant, about 144 TiB.
claims.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
claims.quote: We find that 98.2% of the download traffic in Nostr is wasted, totaling 144 TiB.
claims.read_depth: full page (full PDF text extracted and grepped)
claims.note: Sentence verified verbatim (section 5.4). PARTIAL because it is the authors' computation over crawled posts and the follower graph (per-follower-edge wasted traffic), not network traffic they measured on the wire; I did not audit the method beyond reading the sentence. Intro words it as '98.2% of these retrievals are redundant'. Film wording: 'the authors estimate'.

claims.claim: Capping each post at 10 relays would remove about 78% of replications (potential, before availability trade-off).
claims.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
claims.quote: Further reducing this limit to 10 leads to the removal of an additional 100 million post replications, totaling 480 million (77.9%).
claims.read_depth: full page (full PDF text extracted and grepped)
claims.note: Baseline 616M replications; 480M/616M = 77.9%. It is the 'optimization space' under a cap, with availability impact assessed separately in section 6. Cap at 20 removes 380M (61.7%).

claims.claim: Querying only 5 relays per followed author retained 99.4% of posts in the authors' simulation.
claims.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
claims.quote: even when N is set to 5, it is possible decrease the duplicated retrieval count by 93%, while still achieving 99.4% of post completeness.
claims.read_depth: full page (full PDF text extracted and grepped)
claims.note: Quote is verbatim including the paper's grammar ('possible decrease'). Simulated/data-driven evaluation, not a deployed result. Candidate said 'retrieving from 5 selected relays' - paper: N=5 subset of the user's known relays, completeness over follower graph.

claims.claim: Half of relays were up more than 99% of the time, while about a fifth were down more than 40% of the time.
claims.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
claims.quote: 50% of the relays being available for more than 99% of the specified time period
claims.read_depth: full page (full PDF text extracted and grepped)
claims.note: SURPRISE/CORRECTION: uptime was computed over 2023-10-01 to 2023-12-31 only (last quarter), not the whole July-Dec dataset. Second figure verbatim: 'Approximately 20% of the relays experience downtime for more than 40% of the time.' The paper says most of those are offline for extended periods and never return (the 132 dead relays); with dead relays removed '90% of the relays being operational for more than 80% of the time'. Film must carry this context.

claims.claim: The study identifies 132 relays as dead (offline over a week and still offline at the end).
claims.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
claims.quote: In total, we identify 132 dead relays.
claims.read_depth: full page (full PDF text extracted and grepped)
claims.note: Paper's definition: 'relays that have been offline for more than a week and remain so at the end of our measurements'. Out of 712.

claims.claim: The authors estimate about 95% of free relays cannot cover operating costs from donations alone.
claims.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
claims.quote: our estimates shows 95% of the free-to-use relays cannot cover their operational cost from this alone.
claims.read_depth: full page (full PDF text extracted and grepped)
claims.note: Verbatim from introduction. PARTIAL: it is an estimate; 'this alone' = user donations (zaps); cost benchmark is modelled on Mastodon instance costs (section 4.4). Section text says 'most of the free relays with more than 10 users are unable to cover their operating costs'. Film: 'estimated'.

claims.claim: The paper was accepted to ACM CoNEXT 2025.
claims.title: An Empirical Analysis of the Nostr Social Network: Decentralization, Availability, and Replication Overhead
claims.quote: Accepted to CoNEXT '25: The 21th International Conference on emerging Networking EXperiments and Technologies
claims.read_depth: full page (full PDF text extracted and grepped)
claims.note: Venue is from the arXiv abstract page Comments field (v2 revised 29 Sep 2025; submitted 8 Feb 2024). I did not open the ACM proceedings page, so 'accepted' is the authors' arXiv statement only. Authors at HKUST (Guangzhou).

claims.claim: Delta Chat documentation describes a chatmail relay as a minimal mail server built for instant delivery and enforced security, beyond classic mail servers.
claims.title: Frequently asked questions
claims.quote: A chatmail relay is a minimal Mail Transport Agent (MTA) setup that goes beyond what classic email servers offer
claims.note: Listed properties verbatim: 'Zero State: no private data or metadata collected, messages are auto-deleted'; 'Instant/Realtime: sub-second message delivery'; 'only strict TLS, DKIM and OpenPGP with minimized metadata accepted'. Page footer: Copyright 2025, chatmail collective. Page has no date.

claims.claim: Delta Chat's help says classic email providers generally lack push notifications and chatmail enforces end-to-end encryption.
claims.title: Delta Chat Help (FAQ)
claims.quote: classic email providers will generally not support Push Notifications and have other limitations
claims.our_reading: The relay is kept simple by design in Delta Chat's own words, yet the project still specifies relay properties (instant delivery, push, enforced encryption) - that is our interpretation.
claims.note: Same page: 'chatmail apps and relays pervasively enforce end-to-end encryption and other security standards' and, for self-hosting, 'We generally recommend to set up a chatmail relay.' CORRECTION: the docs do not say 'recommended over ordinary providers' in general; classic addresses are allowed 'only if the email address is used exclusively by chatmail clients'. Also this page itself calls relays 'cheap and dumb servers, that do not store any user data as group states, your name or avatar' - Delta Chat's own word 'dumb' for the relay (opposite framing to the film's 'not dumb' point; use as a fair-comment contrast, with our_reading separate).

claims.claim: Manyverse's maintainer reported initial sync fell from 12 hours to 55 minutes and the database from 2.0 GB to 950 MB over three years.
claims.title: October 2021 update
claims.quote: Initial sync is 13x quicker 3 years ago it would take 12 hours Today it takes 55 minutes
claims.our_reading: Even after 3 years of optimization, first sync was 55 minutes - our reading.
claims.note: Primary post is on manyver.se (the Manyverse project blog by André Staltz), not staltz.com. Same text: 'Database occupies 2x less space (not including blobs) 3 years ago it used 2.0 GB Today it uses 950 MB'. Single-device comparison of Manyverse 3 years earlier vs Oct 2021 with 'the same amount of social content' (his words). He adds '(I am not satisfied with 55 minutes! ...)'. CAVEAT: these figures show improvement through engineering, i.e. a problem that was reduced, not a growth measurement. Quote has bullet line breaks collapsed. Related primary (Aug 2022 update, found via search snippet only for this card, not used as basis): main SSB network grows ~200 MB a year.

claims.claim: Automerge's blog says the Embark essay editor originally took about 40 seconds to load.
claims.title: Merry Commitmas
claims.quote: when we started, loading the editor took around 40 seconds!
claims.note: Context: Embark essay document with ~200,000 operations / ~1000 edit sessions. Date is month shown in the blog index (December 2023); exact day not read. After fixes in Automerge 2.1.10+ 'the load time for the Embark essay is reduced to around ~4 seconds on my machine'.

claims.claim: Automerge's blog says the Embark essay document, with nearly 200,000 edits of history, is 376 KB and loads in a little under 4 seconds.
claims.title: Merry Commitmas
claims.quote: only 376kb and takes a little under 4s to load from disk
claims.note: 'The full edit history is just shy of 200,000 edits.' Author adds this is 'still about 4s too slow'. Single-machine, author's desktop.

claims.claim: Automerge 3.0 announcement: a document that had not loaded after 17 hours loaded in 9 seconds.
claims.title: Automerge 3.0
claims.quote: we recently had an example of a document which hadn’t loaded after 17 hours loading in 9 seconds!
claims.note: WORDING CORRECTION: the page does NOT say 'took 17 hours to load'; it says the document 'hadn’t loaded after 17 hours' (i.e. had not finished). Say 'had not finished loading after 17 hours'. Single anecdotal example, 'documents with large histories'. Same post: memory 'over 10x' lower; pasting Moby Dick: 700Mb (Automerge 2) vs 1.3Mb (Automerge 3). Date is month shown on blog index (July 2025).

claims.claim: Briar released Briar Mailbox, a helper app on a spare always-on Android device, to hold messages while Briar is offline.
claims.title: Briar Mailbox released to improve connectivity
claims.quote: Briar Mailbox is a helper app for Briar messenger that lets you receive encrypted messages from your contacts while Briar is offline.
claims.note: Quote is 21 words. Also: 'leave the Mailbox device connected to power and Wi-Fi'. Briar manual: 'If your contact is offline, your message will be delivered next time you’re both online.' (https://briarproject.org/manual/). 'Why' is given implicitly (users offline at different times; how-it-works page: 'Users who are online at different times can use Briar Mailbox'). Did not read code.briarproject.org.

claims.claim: SSB docs describe 'Pub' nodes at public IPs that improve uptime and availability.
claims.title: Pub
claims.quote: To sync across the Internet, "Pub" nodes run at public IPs and follow users. They are essentially mail-bots which improve uptime and availability.
claims.note: Quote is 24 words. FAQ 'What is a pub?' (https://handbook.scuttlebutt.nz/faq/basics/pub) says without a physical meeting, finding a direct connection 'could be tremendously hard' and pubs 'come in to help'. Page undated.

claims.claim: The SSB Rooms 2.0 spec describes a room as a peer with internet presence that tunnels connections between clients.
claims.title: SSB Rooms 2.0
claims.quote: A room server is an SSB peer with privileged internet presence (for instance, not behind a NAT layer)
claims.note: Revision date 2022-10-10 shown on page. Continues: 'which allows its clients to perform tunneled connections with each other'; room cannot eavesdrop (secret-handshake). The spec gives the mechanism more than a stated 'why'.

claims.claim: Ditto's documentation describes Ditto Server as a cloud component that syncs across disconnected meshes, and calls the platform cloud-optional.
claims.title: Backend Architecture
claims.quote: Ditto Server is a cloud-based component hosted within Ditto’s infrastructure that facilitates data sync across different network scenarios
claims.note: CORRECTION to the card framing: Ditto's own docs say the cloud is optional ('As a cloud-optional data management platform, you get to choose the distributed system architecture' - https://docs.ditto.live/cloud/backend-architecture/cloud-optional-design). They do not say pure P2P failed and a server was then added. Same page: server is 'a central point of coordination and data storage', provides authentication certificates, change data capture and an HTTP API. The doc says 'if a Small Peer has access to the internet, it automatically establishes a connection with Ditto Server'. Does not state a 'why' for needing it. Recommend: use only with 'optional' caveat, or DROP from the 'ended up adding' list.

claims.claim: any-sync's README lists sync, file, consensus and coordinator nodes as network components; self-hosting docs require a network configuration.
claims.title: any-sync
claims.quote: any-sync-node — implementation of a sync node responsible for storing spaces and objects.
claims.note: Verbatim bullet. Also: 'Providers cannot read user information, block users, or alter accounts—they only deliver sync and storage.' and 'Users can choose and switch providers anytime'. Docs (https://doc.anytype.io/anytype/data/sync-and-backup/self-host): 'To back up your channels and data to a self-hosted network, you need to have a network configuration.' PARTIAL: neither page states why a sync node is required; infrastructure role only. Not a statement that P2P alone failed.

claims.claim: Radicle's seeder guide says a peer-to-peer network without seed nodes is feasible but impractical because user nodes go offline.
claims.title: Radicle Seeder Guide
claims.quote: While a peer-to-peer network without seed nodes is feasible, it is impractical.
claims.note: Explanation (verbatim): 'regular “user” nodes go online and offline all the time, so finding a user from which to download a certain piece of content can be challenging, or even impossible if all users with that content are offline.' Best 'why' statement of the five.

claims.claim: The SSB handbook FAQ says an identity cannot currently be used across devices; use on several devices means multiple identities and feeds.
claims.title: Can I use scuttlebutt on different devices, but maintain the same identity?
claims.quote: Currently, you cannot. Identities are tied to a single user on a single device.
claims.note: CANDIDATE CONTRADICTED: official handbook wording does not say 'forks the feed'. I grepped the FAQ page, protocol guide, identity, feed and gossip pages for 'fork': no hit. Official wording: 'You could use scuttlebutt on multiple devices, but you would be maintaining multiple identities and feeds.' The 'fork' mechanism appeared only in search snippets of community posts (viewer.scuttlebot.io, unreachable by me) - NOT used. Protocol guide (https://ssbc.github.io/scuttlebutt-protocol-guide/) says 'Fusion Identities solve the challenge of using multiple devices ... Each device still uses it's own identity, there is no avoiding that'. Page undated and older than the fusion-identity guide, so the FAQ may be stale.
